concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence by contrast clue and synonym pairing

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. Always circumspect, she was reluctant to make judgments, but once arriving at a conclusion, she was ______ in its defense. (A) deferential (B) intransigent (C) lax (D) negligent (E) obsequious (F) resolute

solution.operation: Underline the key phrases "circumspect," "reluctant," and "but once"
solution.result: Three clue phrases, one of which ("but once") is a pivot word
solution.description: Pull out the words the sentence gives you to work with: the two adjectives describing her habitual caution, plus the connector that signals a turn.

solution.operation: Read the clues together to set the sense the blank must carry
solution.result: The blank needs a word that is opposite in some way to "circumspect" and "reluctant"
solution.description: Because the pivot turns the sentence against its opening description, the word in the blank has to describe how firmly she behaves after the caution ends.

solution.operation: Group the six choices into similar-meaning pairs: deferential/obsequious, lax/negligent, intransigent/resolute
solution.description: Sentence equivalence needs two choices that make sentences alike in meaning, so sort the list into pairs before testing any of them against the sentence.

solution.operation: Test "lax" and "negligent" against the required contrast
solution.description: This pair does make two sentences similar in meaning, but it continues the sentiment of the opening clause rather than contrasting with it, so it fails the pivot.

solution.operation: Test "deferential" and "obsequious" against the required contrast
solution.description: This pair is also similar in meaning, but its emphasis on politeness is not the opposite of reluctance and circumspection, so it too fails to pick up the expected contrast.

solution.operation: Test "intransigent" and "resolute" against the required contrast
solution.result: Both fit the logic of the description and create sentences similar in meaning
solution.description: Although not strictly synonymous, the two words both supply the firmness the pivot demands, which is exactly the pair the question asks for.

examples.answer: Choice B: intransigent AND Choice F: resolute

key_reminders: Sentence equivalence needs two choices that both fit the sentence AND yield completed sentences alike in meaning.
A pivot word such as "but" tells you the blank must reverse, not extend, the sense of the earlier clause.
Words need not be strict synonyms to qualify; they only need to make the two sentences mean roughly the same thing.
common_mistakes: Choosing lax/negligent because they form a clean synonym pair, ignoring that they echo rather than contrast with "reluctant."
Choosing deferential/obsequious on the strength of their pairing when their shared sense is politeness, not firmness.
Picking only one word (intransigent or resolute) when the question requires both.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence by synonym pairing and context fit

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. If big sums are to be spent on cleaning up environmental disasters, it is better to spend them on unglamorous but ______ problems such as unsanitary water in Third World countries. (A) futile (B) ephemeral (C) pressing (D) controversial (E) transitory (F) critical

solution.operation: State what the blank must characterize
solution.result: The blank describes the kind of environmental problem that is worth spending large sums on
solution.description: Fix the job of the missing word before looking at choices: it qualifies "problems" in a way that justifies the expenditure.

solution.operation: Scan the six choices for near synonyms
solution.result: Two sets emerge: ephemeral/transitory and pressing/critical
solution.description: Sentence equivalence answers come in pairs, so identify which choices could produce sentences alike in meaning before testing context.

solution.operation: Substitute ephemeral/transitory into the sentence
solution.description: It would be unlikely for anyone to advocate spending large sums on problems that will be quickly gone without any intervention, and unsanitary water would not be characterized as a merely temporary dilemma.

solution.operation: Substitute pressing/critical into the sentence
solution.result: Both fit the context of the rest of the sentence
solution.description: Of the two pairings, only this one makes sense: describing the problems as urgent is what justifies directing the big sums toward them.

solution.operation: Dispose of "futile" and "controversial"
solution.description: Neither has a synonym among the answer choices, so neither can form a required pair, and in addition neither would be used to justify the expenditure of large sums of money.

examples.answer: Choice C: pressing AND Choice F: critical

key_reminders: The correct two choices must both fit the context and produce sentences alike in meaning.
A choice with no synonym partner among the options cannot be part of the answer.
"Unglamorous but ___" signals a positive-value contrast: the word must give a reason to fund the problem.
common_mistakes: Picking ephemeral/transitory simply because they form a tidy synonym pair, without checking that spending big sums on self-resolving problems makes no sense.
Selecting futile or controversial on plausible-sounding tone when neither has a partner to satisfy the alike-in-meaning requirement.

concept.technique_name: critical reasoning inference: must-be-true verified by ratio computation

examples.problem_statement: Gas Mileage. The average fuel efficiency of vehicles sold nationwide during the period 2000-2004 was 25 miles per gallon; the corresponding figure during the period 1995-1999 was 20 miles per gallon. The national average price of gasoline during the period 2000-2004 was $2 per gallon; the corresponding figure during the period 1995-1999 was $1.60 per gallon. The statements above, if true, best support which of the following conclusions? (A) The average fuel efficiency of vehicles sold nationwide should reach 30 miles per gallon for the period 2005-2009. (B) The cost of gasoline for an average trip in a vehicle was higher during the period 1995-1999 than during the period 2000-2004. (C) Rising gasoline prices lead consumers to purchase more fuel-efficient cars. (D) The ratio of average fuel efficiency to average price of gasoline from the 1995-1999 period was roughly equal to the ratio from the 2000-2004 period. (E) Consumers spent more money on gasoline during the period 2000-2004 than during the period 1995-1999.

solution.operation: Classify the question from the stem "best support which of the following conclusions?"
solution.description: The phrase best support could mean Inference or Strengthen, but the stem says the conclusion will be one of the answer choices, which makes it an Inference question.

solution.operation: Record the four given figures in a small table by period
solution.result: Fuel efficiency 20 mpg (95-99) and 25 mpg (00-04); gas price 1.60 dollars per gallon (95-99) and 2 dollars per gallon (00-04)
solution.description: The argument is all facts and figures across two time periods, so a table is the cleanest way to keep the numbers straight.

solution.operation: State the goal for the correct answer
solution.result: Find the choice that must be true from the given data alone
solution.description: With specific averages for two periods and both figures rising over time, expect the answer to rest on a mathematical inference rather than on outside knowledge.

solution.operation: Test (A): projects 30 mpg for 2005-2009
solution.description: Should reach is a prediction about the future, and nothing in the data proves what happens after 2004.

solution.operation: Test (B): cost of gasoline for an average trip was higher in 1995-1999
solution.description: Efficiency was lower in the first period but gas also cost less, and the number or length of trips is unknown, so there is not enough information to prove the comparison.

solution.operation: Test (C): rising prices lead consumers to buy more fuel-efficient cars
solution.description: The statement is logical but unprovable from the argument, which says nothing about why consumers decide to purchase certain cars, and outside knowledge is not allowed.

solution.operation: Test (D) by computing both ratios: 20 / 1.60 = 20 / (8/5) = 400/8 = 12.5 and 25 / 2 = 12.5
solution.description: The claim about ratios can be checked directly with the figures already given, and dividing efficiency by price in each period yields the same value, so the choice must be true.

solution.operation: Test (E): consumers spent more money on gasoline in 2000-2004
solution.description: Average price per gallon is not total money spent; the average price was higher, but people may have bought fewer gallons, especially with better fuel efficiency, so this could be true without having to be true.

key_reminders: An Inference answer must be provable from the stated facts alone - no outside knowledge and no predictions about the future.
"Might be true" is not good enough; eliminate any choice that merely could hold.
A per-unit average (price per gallon) says nothing about a total (money spent) unless quantity is also known.
common_mistakes: Falling for (E) because both gas price and the era feel like higher spending, when total spend needs gallons purchased, not price per gallon.
Accepting (C) as the causal story the two rising figures suggest, though the argument never addresses consumer motives.
Skipping the arithmetic on (D) and dismissing it as a strange-sounding ratio, missing that 20/1.60 and 25/2 both equal 12.5.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion driven by contrast signal words

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. Female labor was essential to the growth of eighteenth-century European textile industries, yet it remains difficult to (i) ______. Despite significant (ii) ______ in research about women, the role of female labor remains the single most glaring omission in most economic analyses of the history of European industrialization. Women far outnumbered men as workers in the textile industries, yet wage indices and discussions of growth, cost of living, and the like (iii) ______ about the male labor force. Blank (i): A track, B overestimate, C ignore. Blank (ii): D advances, E gaps, F disinterest. Blank (iii): G incorporate data only, H suppress most information, I too rarely talk.

solution.operation: Extract the claim of the second sentence
solution.result: The role of women is generally left out of most analyses of industrialization
solution.description: The middle sentence states the passage's central fact, and it is the anchor the other two blanks are measured against.

solution.operation: Apply that omission to Blank (i)
solution.description: Given that the role of women is left out, data about female labor would be hard to come by, making its growth difficult to measure - which is what tracking means here.

solution.operation: Rule out "ignore" and "overestimate" for Blank (i)
solution.description: "Ignore" fails because the author asserts female labor has routinely been overlooked already, and "overestimate" fails because the conjunction "yet" requires a contrast with the importance of female labor rather than an emphasis on it.

solution.operation: Read "Despite" as the signal governing Blank (ii)
solution.description: "Despite" indicates that the larger field of research about women runs counter to the omission, and only advances in that field provide the necessary contrast.

solution.operation: Rule out "gaps" and "disinterest" for Blank (ii)
solution.description: "Gaps" in the larger field would mirror the omission rather than contrast with it, and "disinterest" would explain the omission instead of opposing it.

solution.operation: Read "yet" as the signal governing Blank (iii)
solution.description: The "yet" contrasts the makeup of the workforce with the availability of data about it; since women outnumbered men as workers, the contrast requires data that mostly concerned men.

solution.operation: Rule out "suppress most information" and "too rarely talk" for Blank (iii)
solution.description: The previous sentence says female labor is ignored by economic analyses, so with women excluded the data is mostly about men - it makes no sense to say information about the male labor force is suppressed or too infrequently discussed.

examples.answer: Choice A: track; Choice D: advances; Choice G: incorporate data only

key_reminders: Fill the blank whose sentence carries the most explicit information first, then use it to constrain the others.
"Yet" and "Despite" are contrast signals: the blank must run counter to the clause they attach to.
Every blank must stay consistent with the passage's stated claim that female labor is omitted from the analyses.
common_mistakes: Choosing "ignore" for Blank (i) because the passage is about being ignored, when the sentence needs what is difficult to do, not what is done.
Choosing "gaps" for Blank (ii) because it echoes "omission," missing that "Despite" demands the opposite of an omission.
Choosing "suppress most information" or "too rarely talk" for Blank (iii) by attaching the omission to the male labor force rather than the female one.
